# Education in China
The history of education in China shows an initial focus on improving population-wide literacy in the early years of the People's Republic of China. Since the end of the Cultural Revolution, the system has prioritized economic modernization. Policies have shifted between ideological imperatives and practical efforts, with science and technology education gaining importance in the early 1980s to support the Four Modernizations. The system is structured around a nine-year compulsory education, which mandates six years of primary and three years of secondary education.
Currently, China provides nine-year compulsory education to a large portion of its population, with net elementary school enrollment reaching 98.9 percent. The education system features various levels, including elementary, junior, and senior high school, alongside vocational and technical education. Key policy trends include increasing investment in education, the promotion of lifelong learning, and recent reforms aimed at reducing excessive off-campus tutoring and homework burdens. However, the system faces criticism regarding its intense rigor, emphasis on memorization, and significant quality gaps between urban and rural areas.
